subject: economics
title: Job Seeker Foundations
welcome_lead: Not all unemployment is the same. From between-job searchers to declining factories, learn the labels economists use.
meta_desc: GCSE Economics adventure on unemployment types: frictional, structural, cyclical, seasonal and measures.

concepts.def: Willing/able to work but cannot find a job.
Brief gap between leaving one job and starting another.
Skills don't match jobs available; industry decline.
Tied to time of year (ski instructors, tour guides).
People working PLUS people seeking work.

walkthroughs.body_html: You quit one job on Friday and start a new one in three weeks — those three weeks count as frictional unemployment. It's short-term, voluntary and usually exists even in a booming economy. Job-search apps reduce it.
UK coal mining collapsed in the 1980s. Miners' skills no longer matched new tech jobs in London — they faced structural unemployment. It's long-term and needs retraining or relocation. Tough to fix.
In a recession, AD drops, firms sell less, workers get sacked. This is cyclical unemployment. It rose sharply in 2008–09 and again in 2020. Cured by stimulating AD via fiscal or monetary policy.

options: The sign of XED doesn't matter — only the size does.

Positive XED = substitutes (price of one rises, demand for the other rises); negative XED = complements (price of one rises, demand for the other falls); zero XED = unrelated goods.
